lessons.title: Lesson 13: Sir Alexander Fleming — Patrick Pringle
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension Questions

What great discovery did Fleming make?

Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic drug. He noticed that a mould growing on a culture plate killed bacteria around it. He identified the mould as Penicillium and its juice as penicillin. Penicillin later saved millions of lives from bacterial infections.

How did Fleming's discovery happen?

It happened partly by chance and partly by careful observation. A mould spore fell by accident on a bacterial culture plate. Fleming noticed the clear area where bacteria had been destroyed. Instead of throwing the plate away, he studied it and made his discovery.

What qualities of Fleming does the lesson show?

Fleming was patient, observant and devoted to research. He worked for years without seeking fame or fortune. He shared his discovery freely for the good of mankind. His humility and hard work made him a great scientist.

Book Exercise — Answer These Questions

What are antiseptics and what is the antiseptic method?

Antiseptics are chemical substances which kill germs on wounds and prevent infection. The antiseptic method, introduced by Lister, was to treat wounds and dressings with carbolic acid so that germs could not enter and multiply. Surgeons sprayed carbolic acid in the operating theatre and soaked dressings in it, and the death rate from infected wounds fell sharply. It was the first great attempt to fight the germs that cause wound infection by chemical means.

What was the chief defect of antiseptic method?

The chief defect of the antiseptic method was that the antiseptics killed the living cells of the body as well as the germs. Carbolic acid and similar chemicals destroyed the tissues round a wound and so hindered the natural healing of the body. They also could not reach germs that had already gone deep into the tissues. The method therefore checked infection only at the surface, while damaging the very tissues it was meant to save.

What part is played by the white cells in the blood of a human body?

The white cells in the blood are the body's own soldiers against disease. They gather at the seat of infection, surround the germs and devour them, a process called phagocytosis. They also produce substances that destroy germs and help to wall off infection by forming pus. Fleming's work on penicillin grew out of his interest in these natural defences, since he wanted a substance that would help, not hinder, the white cells.

Give an account of the early life of Fleming.

Alexander Fleming was born in 1881 at Lochfield, a farm in Ayrshire in Scotland, the son of a farmer. He was educated at local schools and at Kilmarnock Academy, and then came to London, where he worked for some years as a shipping clerk. On the advice of his brother he entered St Mary's Hospital Medical School to study medicine, and there he proved a brilliant student. He joined the staff of St Mary's, worked under Sir Almroth Wright on vaccines and immunity, and served as a doctor in the First World War, where infected wounds set him thinking about antiseptics.

Describe how Fleming discovered penicillin.

In 1928 Fleming was working at St Mary's on staphylococcus germs grown on culture plates. One plate had become contaminated by a mould spore that had floated in through the window, and round the mould the germs had been dissolved, leaving a clear zone. Instead of throwing the plate away, Fleming studied it and found that the mould, Penicillium notatum, gave out a juice which killed many kinds of germs. He called this juice penicillin, and thus, by chance joined to careful observation, one of the greatest discoveries in medicine was made.

In what respect is penicillin better than the chemical antiseptics?

Penicillin is better than the chemical antiseptics because it kills germs without harming the cells of the body. Chemical antiseptics destroy living tissue as well as germs and therefore hinder healing, but penicillin leaves the white cells unharmed. It acts even in very weak dilutions and can reach germs inside the body through the blood. It is therefore a natural antibiotic, not a poison, and can be used safely inside the body where antiseptics could never go.

What do you know of the Oxford team?

The Oxford team was led by Professor Howard Florey, with Dr Ernst Chain and Mr Norman Heatley working with him. They took up Fleming's discovery, which had lain unused for ten years, and set themselves to purify penicillin and test it. Working in difficult wartime conditions, they extracted penicillin in pure form and proved by experiments on mice and then on men that it cured infections. Without the Oxford team's patient chemical and medical work, Fleming's mould juice would never have become a usable drug.

How did they make penicillin more effective?

They made penicillin more effective by purifying it and concentrating it, so that a small dose contained great germ-killing power. Heatley devised a method of extracting penicillin from the mould culture and of measuring its strength. They then worked out how to produce it in larger quantities and how to give it by injection so that it reached the infected tissues. Clinical trials showed that purified penicillin, given regularly, could cure septicaemia, pneumonia and infected wounds that had formerly been fatal.

Write a note on penicillin as a wonder drug.

Penicillin is called a wonder drug because it transformed the treatment of bacterial disease within a few years. Wounds that would have become gangrenous, pneumonia, blood poisoning, meningitis and syphilis all yielded to it. In the Second World War it saved the lives of countless soldiers with infected wounds, and in peace it saved mothers from childbed fever and children from deadly infections. It opened the age of antibiotics and added many years to the average length of human life, which is why it is justly called a wonder drug.

Was Fleming proud of his discovery?

No, Fleming was not proud of his discovery; he remained modest about it all his life. He always said that he did not invent penicillin, nature did, and that his part was only to notice what the mould had done. He gave the credit freely to the Oxford team who purified it and to the workers who produced it in quantity. His humility, and his refusal to seek fame or fortune from his discovery, are among the finest qualities the lesson shows in him.

Why couldn't penicillin have been discovered in the research laboratories of America?

Penicillin could not have been discovered in the highly organised research laboratories of America because it was not the product of a planned programme. It came from an accidental contamination of a culture plate in a small, untidy laboratory, noticed by a man with the eye to see its meaning. American laboratories were organised for routine, team research, where a contaminated plate would simply have been thrown away. Fleming's discovery therefore needed the freedom, the mess and the observant mind of a small laboratory, not a great research machine. Fleming's achievement paved the way for other discoveries in the medical field.

What are they?

Fleming's achievement paved the way for the whole family of antibiotics that followed penicillin. Streptomycin was discovered for tuberculosis, and aureomycin, terramycin and other antibiotics followed for many infections. The sulpha drugs and modern chemotherapy grew in the same climate of research into germ-killing substances. Above all, Fleming's work established the idea that nature itself provides weapons against germs, and that idea has guided medical research ever since.

lessons.title: Lesson 14: Louis Pasteur — Margaret Avery
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension Questions

What did Pasteur discover about germs?

Pasteur proved that germs cause fermentation and disease. He showed that germs come from other germs, not from nothing. His experiments disproved the theory of spontaneous generation. He also showed that heat can kill germs, the process called pasteurisation.

How did Pasteur help the silk and wine industries?

Silkworms were dying of disease, and wine was turning sour. Pasteur found that germs caused both troubles. He advised cleanliness and heating to kill the germs. His advice saved the silk industry of France and improved wine-making.

What was Pasteur's greatest service to mankind?

Pasteur developed vaccines against anthrax and rabies. His rabies vaccine saved the life of a boy bitten by a mad dog. He founded the Pasteur Institute for research and treatment. His work laid the foundations of modern medicine and surgery.

Book Exercise — Answer These Questions

Describe the early life of Pasteur.

Louis Pasteur was born in 1822 at Dole in France, the son of a tanner who had served as a soldier under Napoleon. As a boy he was fond of drawing and was not remarkable at school, but he worked hard and won a place at the Ecole Normale in Paris. He became a teacher of chemistry and physics, and then professor at Strasbourg and at Lille, where his work on fermentation began. His early life thus shows a humble, hard-working student rising by patience and devotion to become the greatest scientist of his age.

Give some instances of Pasteur's patriotism.

Pasteur's patriotism showed itself in his refusal of German honours after the Franco-Prussian War, when he returned the honorary degree given him by the University of Bonn. During the war he worked to help his country, and after it he devoted his science to French industries, saving the wine, beer and silk trades. He refused to accept money or honours from Germany and declared that science has no country, but the scientist must have one. His Pasteur Institute in Paris was itself a gift to France, and his whole life was service to his nation as well as to mankind.

What do we mean by spontaneous generation?

By spontaneous generation we mean the old belief that living things can arise by themselves from non-living matter. It was believed that maggots arise from rotting meat, that mice arise from dirty rags, and that germs arise from broth left standing. According to this theory, life is continually being created afresh out of dead matter without parents. Pasteur's experiments were designed to test this belief and, in the end, to disprove it.

How did Pasteur prove that spontaneous generation was not a fact?

Pasteur proved it by his famous swan-neck flask experiments. He boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks, so that air could enter but dust, carrying germs, settled in the bend and could not reach the broth. The broth in these flasks remained clear and lifeless for months, although air had free access to it. When the neck was broken off and dust allowed to fall in, the broth quickly swarmed with germs, proving that germs come from other germs in the air, not from the broth itself.

Describe the importance and popularity of the silkworm industry in France. What help did Pasteur render in curing the silkworm disease in his country?

The silkworm industry was of immense importance in France, giving work to thousands and producing the silk for which France was famous all over the world. In the 1860s a terrible disease, pebrine, followed by flacherie, attacked the silkworms and threatened to ruin the whole industry. Pasteur studied the disease and found that it was caused by tiny germs passed from moth to egg. He advised breeders to destroy every infected moth and keep only eggs from healthy moths, and by this simple method the industry was saved and restored to prosperity.

How did Pasteur discover the treatment for the cattle disease, Anthrax?

Anthrax was a deadly cattle disease that killed sheep and cattle in great numbers and sometimes attacked men as well. Pasteur found that it was caused by a rod-shaped germ, and that animals could be protected by inoculation with a weakened form of the germ. He weakened the anthrax germs by growing them at a high temperature, so that they lost their virulence but still taught the body to resist. At Pouilly-le-Fort in 1881 he publicly vaccinated sheep with his anthrax vaccine, and while the unvaccinated sheep died, the vaccinated lived, proving his treatment.

How did Pasteur discover the method of making vaccines?

Pasteur discovered the method of making vaccines by studying chicken cholera, when an old, forgotten culture was used by accident. Chickens inoculated with the old, weakened culture became ill but recovered, and afterwards resisted a fresh, strong dose that killed unprotected birds. He realised that a germ weakened by age, heat or air could give protection without causing the full disease. This principle of attenuation, of weakening the germ to make a safe vaccine, became the basis of all his later vaccines and of modern preventive medicine.

Give an account of Pasteur's treatment of Hydrophobia and how he cured the first patient suffering from it.

Hydrophobia, or rabies, is the terrible disease caused by the bite of a mad dog, and in Pasteur's day it was always fatal. Pasteur prepared a vaccine by passing the virus through rabbits and drying the infected spinal cords, so that the virus grew weaker day by day. In 1885 a boy, Joseph Meister, bitten badly by a rabid dog, was brought to him, and Pasteur gave him a series of injections of increasing strength over ten days. The boy lived, and the cure astonished the world, bringing sufferers from every country to Paris and leading to the founding of the Pasteur Institute.

How did Pasteur show the way to other scientists? Give an account of the discoveries.

Pasteur showed the way to other scientists by establishing the germ theory of disease and fermentation. Lister, following Pasteur, introduced antiseptic surgery, and surgeons learned to kill germs before they entered wounds. Other scientists, following his vaccine principle, made vaccines against cholera, typhoid, diphtheria and tetanus. His work on pasteurisation, the heating of milk and wine to kill germs, and his founding of the Pasteur Institute, made him the father of modern microbiology and preventive medicine.

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Mustafa Kamal — Wilfrid F. Castle
lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension Questions

Who was Mustafa Kamal? What did he achieve?

Mustafa Kamal, later Ataturk, was the founder of modern Turkey. He led the Turks against foreign occupation after the First World War. He won independence and established the Turkish Republic. He then reformed Turkey into a modern, secular nation.

What reforms did Mustafa Kamal introduce in Turkey?

He abolished the Caliphate and separated religion from the state. He gave women equal rights, including the right to vote. He replaced Arabic script with the Latin alphabet for Turkish. He introduced Western dress, law and education in Turkey.

What qualities made Mustafa Kamal a great leader?

He was brave, determined and far-sighted. He loved his country and worked selflessly for its freedom. He was a soldier, a statesman and a reformer in one. His leadership transformed a defeated empire into a proud republic.

Book Exercise — Answer These Questions

What was the attitude of the Turkish government towards the Allies after World War I?

After the First World War the Turkish government at Istanbul, under Sultan Mehmed VI, adopted an attitude of submission towards the Allies. It accepted the Allied occupation of Istanbul and the partition of the Ottoman Empire, and it obeyed Allied orders. The Sultan's government hoped to save the throne by cooperating with the victors, even at the cost of the country's independence. This submissive attitude angered the Turkish patriots, who refused to accept a peace that dismembered their homeland.

Why was Mustafa Kamal sent to Anatolia?

Mustafa Kamal was sent to Anatolia officially to supervise the disbanding of the Turkish army and to restore order there. The Sultan's government, acting under Allied pressure, wanted the remaining Turkish forces in Anatolia dissolved. Kamal was chosen as inspector of the army in Anatolia because of his reputation as a soldier. In fact, once in Anatolia, he used his mission to organise the national resistance instead of carrying out the Sultan's orders.

What was the reaction of the Turkish patriots to the intention of the Allies to partition the Ottoman Empire?

The Turkish patriots reacted with anger and determination against the Allied intention to partition the Ottoman Empire. They refused to accept a settlement that would give Smyrna to Greece, large areas to France and Italy, and leave Turkey a small state round Istanbul. National congresses at Erzurum and Sivas declared that the country must remain whole and that the nation itself would decide its fate. The patriots rallied round Mustafa Kamal and prepared to resist the partition by force of arms.

Write a note on Mustafa Kamal's activities in Anatolia.

In Anatolia Mustafa Kamal organised the national movement from nothing into a powerful force. He called the congresses of Erzurum and Sivas, which united the patriots and declared the national will. He set up the Grand National Assembly at Ankara in 1920, which became the government of the national resistance. He raised and trained an army, directed the War of Independence against the Greeks and the Allies, and laid the foundations of the new Turkish Republic.

Why did Mehmed order Mustafa Kamal to return to Constantinople?

Mehmed ordered Mustafa Kamal to return to Constantinople because he feared Kamal's growing power in Anatolia. The Sultan saw that Kamal was not disbanding the army but organising a national movement that challenged the authority of Istanbul. Under Allied pressure, and wishing to keep control of the country, Mehmed dismissed Kamal from his post and ordered him back. The order was meant to remove the leader of the resistance and to break the national movement before it grew stronger.

What was Mustafa Kamal's reply?

Mustafa Kamal's reply was to resign from the army rather than obey the order to return. He gave up his rank and uniform so that the Sultan could no longer command him as an officer. As a civilian he continued to lead the national movement with even greater freedom. His reply thus turned dismissal into defiance, and showed that he would serve the nation, not the Sultan's government.

How did Mehmed try to regain Anatolia for himself?

Mehmed tried to regain Anatolia by sending his own forces against the nationalists and by relying on the Allies. The government at Istanbul issued decrees against Kamal, raised an army of its own, and sought Allied help to crush Ankara. It also used religious authority against the nationalists, declaring them rebels against the Caliph. But the people of Anatolia supported Kamal, the Sultan's forces failed, and Istanbul lost all authority over the interior of the country.

Why did his plan fail?

Mehmed's plan failed because the nation stood behind Mustafa Kamal and not behind the Sultan. The people of Anatolia had suffered under occupation and partition, and they trusted Kamal's leadership and his army. The Sultan's forces were weak, divided and without popular support, while the national army grew stronger every month. Above all, the victories of the national army over the Greeks destroyed the last hope of Istanbul, and the Sultan's authority collapsed.

What were the terms offered to Turkey by the Allies?

The terms offered to Turkey by the Allies were contained in the Treaty of Sevres of 1920. Turkey was to lose Smyrna and western Anatolia to Greece, large areas in the south to France and Italy, and the Arab provinces altogether. The Turkish army was to be limited to a small force, the Straits were to be internationalised, and Turkey was to pay heavy reparations. In effect Turkey would have become a small, dependent state, and it was these terms that the national movement refused to accept.

Give an account of the Greek attack and its defeat.

The Greeks, encouraged by the Allies, landed at Smyrna in 1919 and advanced deep into Anatolia, hoping to destroy the national movement. At first they made progress, but Mustafa Kamal organised the Turkish army and halted them at the Battle of Sakarya in 1921. In August 1922 he launched a great counter-offensive at Dumlupinar, broke the Greek lines and drove the Greek army in rout to the sea. Smyrna was recovered, the Greek invasion was destroyed, and Turkey's victory forced the Allies to make a new and honourable peace at Lausanne.

Give an account of the departure of Mehmed from Istanbul.

When the national army triumphed, the Sultanate was abolished by the Grand National Assembly in November 1922. Mehmed VI, deserted by his ministers and fearing for his life, left Istanbul secretly. He fled on a British warship, abandoning his capital, his throne and his country. His departure marked the end of the Ottoman dynasty and the final victory of the national movement under Mustafa Kamal.

Describe the reforms introduced by Mustafa Kamal with reference to: (i) the position of women, (ii) removal of illiteracy, (iii) change in dresses, (iv) adoption of the Roman script and (v) the industrial and economic development.

For women, Mustafa Kamal gave them equal rights with men: they were unveiled, educated, admitted to professions and given the vote. For illiteracy, he opened schools everywhere, made primary education free and compulsory, and himself taught the new alphabet to the people. For dress, he abolished the fez and the veil and introduced Western dress, so that Turks dressed like modern Europeans. For script, he replaced the Arabic script with the Roman script in 1928, making Turkish easy to read and learn. For industry and economy, he built railways, factories, banks and mines, encouraged agriculture and trade, and laid the foundations of a modern national economy.

Sum up in a few sentences the work of Mustafa Kamal as a great nation-builder.

Mustafa Kamal saved Turkey from partition and foreign occupation and made it an independent republic. He abolished the Sultanate and the Caliphate, separated religion from the state, and gave Turkey a modern constitution. He reformed education, law, dress, script and the position of women, and built up industry and agriculture. As soldier, statesman and reformer he transformed a defeated empire into a proud, modern nation, and for this he is rightly called Ataturk, the father of the Turks.

lessons.notes_html:
Comprehension Questions

Note: the source PDF marks its comprehension selection for this lesson as superseded (dialogue mismatch) — it describes a different dialogue about examinations, not the Farasat–Saleem dialogue on child abuse in the book exercise below — so it is not reproduced here.

Book Exercise — Answer These Questions

What type of news was there in the newspaper?

The newspaper carried news of another incident of child abuse in that very week. Farasat, reading the newspaper in the college library, exclaimed at the fresh incident, and Saleem took the paper in alarm. The news was of the tragic kind that had led to mass protest, and it left both students sad and thoughtful. It was this news that started the whole discussion with their teacher about the menace of child abuse.

Why did Farasat and Saleem become sad after reading the news?

Farasat and Saleem became sad because the news told of a child who had suffered abuse, one more in a series of tragic incidents. They were shocked that such cruelty could happen in their own city and to innocent children. Their teacher found them sitting pensively in the library, quite dejected, and asked whether everything was all right. Their sadness was the natural pity of young men faced with the suffering of children who cannot defend themselves.

Describe the four categories of the child abuse.

The teacher explains that child abuse means maltreatment of a child and can be categorised into four categories. The first is neglect, when a child is left without food, care or protection. The second is emotional abuse, when a child is frightened, humiliated or denied love. The third is physical abuse, when a child is beaten or injured, and the fourth is sexual abuse, when a child is used for sexual purposes.

How can we overcome child abuse?

Child abuse can be overcome by the combined effort of the family, the school, the government and society. Parents should give their children love, care, education and a safe home, and teachers should watch for signs of abuse and report them. The government should strengthen child protection institutions, enforce the law against abusers, and give free and compulsory education. Above all, people must gain knowledge about the problem, share information, and strive to create a world in which children only need to focus on living happily.

What are the basic rights of children in Islam?

In Islam children are regarded as gifts and a trust from Allah, and Islam pays particular attention to their rights. Children have the right to be fed, clothed and protected until they reach adulthood. The child has the right to good education and a stable environment in which to grow. The teacher closes the dialogue with a hadith of the Holy Prophet, that he is not one of us who does not have mercy on our young ones and does not respect our elders.

What are the threats to the children living in war-zones of the world?

Children living near war-zones face many threats, beginning with child casualties from explosive weapons, which children mistake for toys. Explosives limit access to safe places for children and their families, and children as young as eight join military groups, forced by poverty, to defend their community or for revenge. Refugee and migrant children face kidnapping, and many become slaves, soldiers and drug traffickers. Lack of access to quality education is another threat, and extreme poverty brings malnutrition and stunting in the new generation.

How can parents, teachers and media perform their duties to eliminate this evil of child abuse from the society?

Parents should get their children educated and consider it the top priority of their life, for educating a girl child is educating a nation. Teachers can play a very important role in reporting child abuse, teaching youngsters that danger may lurk among people they love and trust, and alerting parents. The media is equally involved in eliminating child abuse and promoting a conducive environment for child safety, and social media, though it changes communication, must be watched by parents for its good and bad effects on children. The government should strengthen institutions such as families of children in vulnerable circumstances, social welfare departments and law enforcement agencies, so that a teacher who sees bruises can report to social welfare, which investigates before reporting to the law and ultimately to the court.

As young as fifteen
As young as eighteen
As young as eight
mcqs.why: The notes list the threats to children in war-zones and state that children as young as eight join military groups, forced by poverty, to defend their community or for revenge.

mcqs.q: What does the dialogue say about educating a girl child?
options: Educating a girl child is educating a nation
Educating a girl child is a waste of money
Educating a girl child is the duty of the state only
Educating a girl child matters less than educating a boy
mcqs.why: The notes say parents should get their children educated as the top priority of their life, for educating a girl child is educating a nation; teachers can report abuse and alert parents, and the media must promote a safe environment for children.
